newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Czech tourism surges but visitors go home sooner.
newsitem.headline: Czech tourism surges but visitors go home sooner.

text.p: The Czech Republic continued to attract tourists in record numbers in 1996, but they stayed for shorter periods of time, hitting top class hotels and landlords, official figures showed on Tuesday.
The Czech Statistical Bureau (CSU) said the number of foreign visits, measured by border police, rose by nearly 12 percent from 1995 to 109.4 million.
But a survey conducted by GfK Praha for the Czech Tourism Centre, showed a decline in the average length of stay in the country by tourists to 2.75 days from 3.09 in 1995.

"The average stay fell, above all, among tourists using rented apartments, rented rooms and hotels in the highest categories," it said adding there had been a corresponding rise in occupancy at lower accommodation categories.

Despite the bad news for hoteliers and landlords, the Czech government, which relies heavily on tourism revenues to boost balance of payments, can take heart from a rise in average daily expenditure to $35.02 from $29.54 in 1995.
Vistors also appear undeterred by the country's reputation for surly service and dishonest taxi drivers, though the biggest visitor complaint was about criminality.
The survey showed that approximately three quarters of foreign visitors in 1996 had travelled to the Czech Republic previously, with about half there for their sixth or more trip.
While tourists worldwide continue to flock to the Czech Republic, Czechs themselves are travelling abroad in greater numbers.
Their trips hit net Czech income from tourism, which is expected to fall to $1.1 billion in 1996 from $1.25 billion in 1995, the Ministry for Local Development said in January.
In 1996, Czechs made 48.6 million foreign trips, up 8.3 percent from 1995, the CSU reported.

The Local Development Ministry said recently that total 1996 revenues from tourism should rise by 32 percent to $3.8 billion, while Czech spending abroad was seen rising by 65.6 percent to $2.7 billion. -- Prague Newsroom, 42-2-2423-0003
